issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, 'being forced to do something' and tactile body-state cues are plausible triggers, but 'burnt smell' introduces a danger cue more typical of fire/explosion trauma and is not supported by the other selected items. It feels disconnected from the stated trauma and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is otherwise self-blaming/defectiveness-focused and tightly linked to triggers, but 'fear of rage' shifts to fear of one's own future violent loss of control. That theme is not supported by the trauma type, the other appraisals, or the maladaptive strategies, making this item difficult to integrate into the same formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time; Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
issues.explanation: The memory items indicate highly severe, here-and-now re-experiencing, which is plausible at this PCL-5 level, but they sit awkwardly with the formulation because Memory has only a weak link to Negative Appraisals and no active links to Triggers or Maladaptive Strategies. Selecting two very strong reliving items plus disorganized narration makes Memory appear more central than the formulation suggests.

vignette: Thida, a thirty-five-year-old physical therapist of South Eastern Asian descent, had navigated two years of severe psychological distress, her symptom burden clearly reflected in a PCL-5 score of 79. The trauma originated during a violent confrontation with her former partner, who physically pinned her to the ground and twisted her arms behind her back. During the assault, the biting cold of the hallway tile against her cheek and the absolute loss of autonomy became inextricably fused to his grip. When she later attempted to process the incident, the memory would not settle as a historical event; instead, it felt as though it were happening right now, flooding her with such overwhelming emotion that she would have to stop mid-sentence, losing the thread entirely when trying to explain what happened. This vivid, uncontainable reliving cemented her core beliefs: she felt permanently humiliated by the violation, convinced there was something fundamentally defective about her as a person, and convinced the event happened entirely because of the way she had acted. Over the following months, these appraisals began warping her daily clinical environment. In her rehabilitation center, where adjusting a patient's shoulder or checking spinal alignment required steady, contact-heavy work, a colleague's accidental brush against her elbow would immediately ignite a spike of self-blame and humiliation. That acute sense of defectiveness and shame then propelled her into rigid maladaptive patterns: she began mentally scanning every corridor for men who looked aggressive, and she spent hours dwelling on how the event could have been prevented. The cycle quickly tightened as her internal warnings dictated her physical reality. The constant conviction that she was permanently humiliated and broken turned ordinary sensations into alarms; a glass of water left too cold on her treatment desk felt like a direct threat to her autonomy, and any request that sounded directive made her throat close up as if her wrists were being bound again. Her relentless prevention rumination and hypervigilance toward people meant she could never truly relax, and her heightened state of alertness kept her body braced for the very temperatures and physical intrusions she dreaded, ensuring the triggers remained sharp and immediate. By the time Thida walked into the intake clinic, her marriage had grown strained by her withdrawal. Her husband's attempts to comfort her with a hand on her shoulder now felt like a cage, and she had learned to flinch before he could even reach for her. She sought help not because she wanted to forget, but because the weight of convincing herself that something was irrevocably wrong had made her unable to function at work or at home. Most of all, she was terrified that the shame would never lift, that she would spend the rest of her life braced for the next grip, the next chill, the next moment she might be forced to yield. Yet, sitting on the edge of the chair, she held onto a fragile hope that understanding the trap might finally give her back the agency she had lost.
